verses.text: Samson went to Gaza, and saw there a prostitute, and went in to her.

The Gazites were told, “Samson is here!” They surrounded him, and laid wait for him all night in the gate of the city, and were quiet all the night, saying, “Wait until morning light, then we will kill him.”

Samson lay until midnight, and arose at midnight, and laid hold of the doors of the gate of the city, and the two posts, and plucked them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders, and carried them up to the top of the mountain that is before Hebron.
It came to pass afterward, that he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.

The lords of the Philistines came up to her, and said to her, “Entice him, and see in which his great strength lies, and by what means we may prevail against him, that we may bind him to afflict him; and we will each give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me where your great strength lies, and what you might be bound to afflict you.”
Samson said to her, “If they bind me with seven green cords that were never dried, then shall I become weak, and be as another man.”
Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green cords which had not been dried, and she bound him with them.

Now she had an ambush waiting in the inner room. She said to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” He broke the cords, as a string of tow is broken when it touches the fire. So his strength was not known.
Delilah said to Samson, “Behold, you have mocked me, and told me lies: now please tell me with which you might be bound.”
He said to her, “If they only bind me with new ropes with which no work has been done, then shall I become weak, and be as another man.”
So Delilah took new ropes, and bound him therewith, and said to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” The ambush was waiting in the inner room. He broke them off his arms like a thread.
Delilah said to Samson, “Until now, you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me with what you might be bound.” He said to her, “If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web.”
She fastened it with the pin, and said to him, “The Philistines are on you, Samson!” He awakened out of his sleep, and plucked away the pin of the beam, and the web.
She said to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and have not told me where your great strength lies.”
When she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, his soul was troubled to death.

He told her all his heart, and said to her, “No razor has ever come on my head; for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, then my strength will go from me, and I will become weak, and be like any other man.”

When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called for the lords of the Philistines, saying, “Come up this once, for he has told me all his heart.” Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her, and brought the money in their hand.
She made him sleep on her knees; and she called for a man, and shaved off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him.
She said, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke out of his sleep, and said, “I will go out as at other times, and shake myself free.” But he didn’t know that Yahweh had departed from him.
The Philistines laid hold on him, and put out his eyes; and they brought him down to Gaza, and bound him with fetters of brass; and he ground at the mill in the prison.
However the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaved.
The lords of the Philistines gathered them together to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, and to rejoice; for they said, “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hand.”
When the people saw him, they praised their god; for they said, “Our god has delivered our enemy and the destroyer of our country, who has slain many of us, into our hand.”
When their hearts were merry, they said, “Call for Samson, that he may entertain us.” They called for Samson out of the prison; and he performed before them. They set him between the pillars;
and Samson said to the boy who held him by the hand, “Allow me to feel the pillars whereupon the house rests, that I may lean on them.”
Now the house was full of men and women; and all the lords of the Philistines were there; and there were on the roof about three thousand men and women, who saw while Samson performed.
Samson called to Yahweh, and said, “Lord Yahweh, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once, God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.”
Samson took hold of the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and leaned on them, the one with his right hand, and the other with his left.

Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He bowed himself with all his might; and the house fell on the lords, and on all the people who were therein. So the dead that he killed at his death were more than those who he killed in his life.

Then his brothers and all the house of his father came down, and took him, and brought him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial site of Manoah his father. He judged Israel twenty years.

footnotes.content: Samson, strong in body but wandering in heart, goes to Gaza seeking a woman. How often do we know what we ought not to do, and do it anyway? The Lord's gift of strength cannot shield us from the harvest we sow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Gazites plan an ambush through the night. But notice—they wait. They cannot move against him openly; they must hide and scheme. Even his enemies know his strength is not their strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At midnight Samson tears the gates from their posts and carries them to the hilltop. The picture is almost comic—mighty strength at work—yet we sense the tragedy: his strength is still his only language. He does not yet know how to be weak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He loved Delilah. The phrase is short but heavy—not love, but the pull of desire. And Delilah's valley is literal, but also spiritual: lower ground. The heart that seeks itself will find itself in low places.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistine lords offer silver—always silver. They know what moves a heart toward betrayal. Delilah listens, and the price is set. She will sell him, not for love, but for silver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Tell me your secret," she says tenderly. Such a simple question, wrapped in affection. How many of us have learned the hard way that not every gentle voice is faithful?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samson lies—his first answer to a trap is a falsehood. Already his discernment is clouded. A man who cannot see that his beloved is the enemy is a man who cannot see truly at all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She binds him with the cords he named. She acts swiftly; she already has accomplices waiting. Delilah does not love; she executes a plan. And Samson, for all his strength, does not see it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The Philistines are on you!" she cries. He snaps the cords like tinder. Yet his strength fails to teach him—he does not flee, does not pray, does not recognize the trap. Pride keeps him bound longer than any cord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again she accuses him of mocking her, of lying. She makes him feel guilty for not trusting her. How cruel: to turn his strength into shame and his caution into heartlessness. This is how betrayal works.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A second lie, a second test. He offers a new secret, hoping perhaps to satisfy her, to prove his love. But a heart bent on using another cannot be satisfied—only fed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again the ambush. Again the trap is sprung. And again Samson breaks free—his physical strength still sure, but his soul increasingly enslaved. How many times must a man be trapped before he asks why?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A third lie, woven into an intimate act—his hair braided with hers. He mingles his secret with her touch. Yet even now, the cord of deceit binds tighter than any rope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He wakes and shakes it all away—the web, the pin, her fingers. But she has learned his pattern now. She knows that time and repetition work where cunning alone has failed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "How can you say you love me?" The cruelest test: she uses the language of love as a weapon. Three times he has lied to her; now she counts them back with tears and blame. His strength becomes his shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daily she presses him. Daily the words, the tears, the accusation. His soul is troubled unto death. How gently the Scripture describes the work of a deceiver—not a shout, but a whisper repeated until the will grows weary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tells her all his heart: a Nazirite from the womb, his hair uncut, his covenant with the Lord unbroken. And when he speaks this sacred truth to the one bent on betraying him, he seals his own downfall. The most holy things should be guarded in the most faithful hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She sees that he has emptied himself before her—all his heart laid bare. Immediately she summons the lords and the silver. The moment he confesses his secret is the moment she betrays him. Love was never her aim.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She lulls him to sleep upon her knees—the deepest intimacy turned to vulnerability. A man is called; the razor does its work. In a moment, the vow of a lifetime is undone, and his strength flows from him like water.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He wakes and tries to shake himself free as before. But this time there is no breaking free. "The Lord had departed from him"—the most terrible knowledge a man can have. We may not notice the moment grace withdraws, but we always notice the silence that follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His eyes put out, his body bound, his strength now slavery—grinding at the mill. The mighty deliverer becomes the slave. What Samson's strength could not teach him, his blindness now reveals: he was never his own strength's master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In captivity, in darkness, in humiliation—his hair begins to grow again. A small sign of mercy, undeserved. And here is the deep grace: even in chains, the Lord does not forget His covenant. The restoration begins in the prisoner's cell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistines gather at the temple of Dagon to celebrate their victory. Yet they mistake their fortune for the defeat of the Lord—a fatal error. Those who forget that every breath is God's own cannot see His hand until it falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Our god has delivered our enemy into our hand." They praise Dagon for what they believe is victory. But false gods cannot deliver, and false praise builds on sand. The real deliverance—and judgment—is yet to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their hearts merry, they call for him to entertain them. Samson the mighty is now Samson the plaything, forced to perform for mockery. And yet—notice—they position him between the pillars that hold the house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He asks the boy's help to feel the pillars. A blind man, once mighty, now seeking the help of a child to stand. Yet in that moment of deepest need, he prays—and his prayer opens the way to redemption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The house is full—thousands gathered to see the strong man brought low. The scene is set for what seems like complete humiliation. But God sees further than any eye in that crowd.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once." In blindness and chains, with his strength gone, Samson calls on the Lord—not for escape, but for one final act of justice. At last, he asks not for his will, but for God's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He takes hold of the two pillars—his hands, once wielded in pride, now instruments of God's judgment. In his surrender, his strength returns—not for himself, but for the deliverance of his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this moment: a life spent in the service of self, yet redeemed in the end by a cry to God. Samson's final prayer—brief, humble, asking only for God's strength—speaks to what we too might become when we stop running from the One who sees us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His brothers carry him home, and they lay him in the tomb of Manoah—buried with his people, in the place of his fathers. He judged Israel twenty years. A broken man, redeemed by one faithful moment, rested at last in the arms of his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
